title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: In the slanting evening shadows thrown by the luggage piled up on the platform, Vronsky — in his long overcoat and slouch hat, hands in his pockets — paced up and down like a caged animal, turning sharply every twenty paces. As Sergey Ivanovitch came toward him, he had the impression Vronsky had seen him but was pretending not to. It made no difference at all to Sergey Ivanovitch. He had risen above any personal feeling about Vronsky.

At that moment Sergey Ivanovitch regarded Vronsky as a man taking on an important role in a great cause, and Koznishev felt it was his duty to encourage him and let him know he approved. He walked up to him.
Vronsky stopped, looked at him hard, recognized him, and stepped a few paces forward to meet him, shaking his hand warmly.
"You may not have wanted to see me," said Sergey Ivanovitch, "but couldn't I be useful to you in some way?"
"There's no one I'd less mind seeing than you," Vronsky said. "Forgive me — there's nothing in life left that I do want."

"I understand completely. I only meant to offer my help," said Sergey Ivanovitch, studying Vronsky's face, which carried unmistakable signs of suffering. "Would a letter to Ristitch — to Milan — be useful?"

"Oh, no!" said Vronsky, as if he were having trouble following. "If you don't mind, let's keep walking. It's too stuffy near the carriages. A letter? No, thank you — you don't need a letter of introduction to go meet death. And not for the Turks either —" he said, with a smile that was only on his lips. His eyes kept their look of angry pain.

"Yes — but a connection like that might make it easier to get in touch with the people you'll need to work with. Still, suit yourself. I was very glad to hear what you intend to do. The volunteers have been attacked from every side, and a man like you raises the whole effort in the public's eyes."

"My value as a man," Vronsky said, "is that my life is worth nothing to me. And that I still have enough physical strength to cut my way into their ranks and either trample them or fall. That much I know. I'm glad there's something I can spend my life on, since to me it isn't just useless, it's hateful. Anyone is welcome to it." And his jaw twitched impatiently from the steady gnawing of his toothache, which kept him from even speaking with his normal expression.

"You'll become another man — I'm sure of it," Sergey Ivanovitch said, moved. "To deliver your fellow men from slavery is an aim worth dying and living for. May God grant you outward success — and inward peace," he added, and held out his hand. Vronsky pressed it warmly.
"Yes — as a weapon I may still be of some use. But as a man, I'm finished," he forced out.

He could barely speak through the throbbing in his strong teeth, which sat in his mouth like rows of ivory. He was silent, his eyes fixed on the wheels of the tender as they rolled smoothly along the rails.

And suddenly a different pain — not a physical ache but an inner anguish that gripped his whole being — made him forget the toothache for an instant. As he looked at the tender and the rails, with the conversation he had just had with someone he hadn't seen since his disaster, he remembered _her_ — that is, what was left of her when he had run, half out of his mind, into the cloakroom of the railway station — sprawled shamelessly on the table among strangers, the blood-stained body that had been so full of life only a moment before; the head untouched, falling back under the weight of its hair, the curls at the temples, the exquisite face, the half-open red mouth, the strange fixed expression — pitiful on the lips and terrible in the still-open eyes — that seemed to be repeating that awful phrase she had said when they were fighting: that he would be sorry for this.

He tried to picture her the way she had been when they first met, also at a railway station — mysterious, lovely, in love, seeking happiness and giving it, not cruelly vengeful the way he remembered her at the end. He tried to call up his best moments with her, but those moments were poisoned forever. The only image he could hold was of her triumphant — having made good on her threat to lay on him a remorse that could never be cleared. He stopped feeling the toothache; his face was working with sobs.
After walking past the baggage twice more in silence and getting hold of himself, he turned back to Sergey Ivanovitch and spoke calmly:
"Have you had any telegrams since yesterday's? Yes — driven back for a third time, but a decisive engagement is expected for tomorrow."
They talked a little more about King Milan's proclamation and the huge impact it could have, then parted as the second bell rang, each heading to his own carriage.
